\paragraph{No significant improvement over greedy.}
We evaluate significance via 2-seed instance-level sign tests ($n{=}551$, Fisher combination).
On NER, the oracle (0.778) reveals 13.3~pp of headroom above greedy (0.645).
LP achieves the highest mean selection F1 (0.647), indistinguishable from greedy ($\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$); all other signals also fail to reach significance (all $p{>}0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}), with 75--80\% of instances producing identical F1 under signal selection and greedy.
On RE, the best signal (LP, 0.395) falls below greedy (0.404, $-0.9$\,pp; single seed, preliminary), while 18.1~pp of oracle headroom remains.
VC, the best quality estimator ($\rho{=}0.379$), selects to only 0.623 on NER ($\Delta{=}{-}2.2$~pp, $p{=}0.26$); the direction is consistent with CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}), though CoNLL's limited oracle headroom (${\leq}4.0$~pp at $N{=}8$) constrains selection comparison.

\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
Instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} is best; when per-sample variance is low, even perfect quality estimation fails to discriminate.
Individual seeds exhibit notable variance (even the best seed $p{=}0.19$), motivating multi-seed evaluation.
Closing this gap likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and selecting via agreement---yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but information extraction (IE) produces \textit{sets} of entities and relations with partial overlap, where no majority vote exists.
Can confidence signals still guide selection in this structured setting?

We compare five confidence signals---spanning structural consistency, surface agreement, and model-internal families---across three NER benchmarks and one RE benchmark (preliminary) with two 8B-parameter models.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation yet none significantly improves best-of-$N$ sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
The gap has two layers: instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction, and log-probability---the only per-sample signal---is too compressed within instances to discriminate; a free-form decoding ablation confirms this compression is intrinsic to the model, not an artifact of constrained decoding.
Signal rankings shift with task difficulty and collapse at the capability boundary.
Closing the gap likely requires learned per-sample scoring such as trained verifiers.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
4	On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
5	More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
6	These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
7	For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
8	But information extraction (IE) poses a structurally different challenge.
9	The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
10	There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
11	Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?
12	
13	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
14	Self-consistency methods for reasoning \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
15	\citet{yao2026consistency} examine consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE; our work extends theirs with structural matching, a selection analysis, and a difficulty gradient.
16	
17	All experiments use constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}, the standard for schema-compliant IE output.\footnote{Our free-form ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms fine-tuned models produce 99.95\% valid JSON without grammar constraints.}
18	
19	Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): consistency signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) but fail at sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom.
20	Four of five signals are instance-level by construction; log-probability, the only per-sample signal, is too compressed to discriminate (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), though where compression is mitigated, selection recovers gains (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
21	
22	\begin{figure*}[t]
23	\centering
24	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
25	\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: high inter-sample agreement correlates with high F1 (quality estimation). \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates, precluding sample selection.}
26	\label{fig:overview}
27	\end{figure*}
28	
29	We compare five confidence signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
30	Our contributions are:
31	\begin{enumerate}
32	    \item \textbf{Metric dissociation.}
33	    We find that quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection decouple, so single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
34	
35	    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap.}
36	    Despite strong quality estimation, no signal improves sample selection: log-probability scores are too compressed within instances, and MBR-style selection correlates with F1 across but not within instances.
37	
38	    \item \textbf{Difficulty- and task-dependent signal rankings.}
39	    Signal rankings shift with task complexity and type, and collapse at the capability boundary. RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
40	\end{enumerate}
41	
42

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
4	Self-consistency decoding \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning by majority voting over chain-of-thought samples, assuming a discrete answer space.
5	Extensions to free-form text use LLM-based comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, atomic sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or cross-sample hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
6	For test-time scaling \cite{zhang2025tts}, \citet{snell2025scaling} characterize compute scaling laws and \citet{brown2024monkeys} show best-of-$N$ gains across tasks.
7	Recent reward-free selectors include confidence-weighted voting \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc}, KL-based self-certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty}, adaptive sampling \cite{kim2026reasc}, ranked aggregation \cite{wang2025rankedvoting}, and latent-space consistency \cite{oh2025latentsc}.
8	Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings, echoing our finding that signal rankings shift with task complexity; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on output fusion rather than confidence-based selection.
9	All of the above target reasoning/QA with discrete answers or specific aggregation strategies.
10	Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap: strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$).
11	
12	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
13	\citet{yao2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE, corroborating our quality-estimation findings.
14	Their work leaves open three questions we address: (i)~whether structural matching improves on surface-level agreement (which they acknowledge ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs''); (ii)~whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection; and (iii)~whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient.
15	Soft Jaccard, the structural consistency measure used in our analysis, addresses (i) through type-aware bipartite matching with token-level span overlap; our selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) directly addresses (ii); and our three-dataset evaluation spanning easy (CoNLL) to hard (SciERC) tasks addresses (iii).
16	CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses model confidence with inter-sample consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction.
17	Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, josifoski2022genie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, wang2023instructuie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
18	Soft Jaccard uses standard tools (bipartite matching, token IoU) and is not itself a contribution; the contribution is the systematic comparison revealing when structural signals outperform surface-level agreement.
19	
20	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
21	Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, selective abstention \cite{wen2025know}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs.
22	Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly.
23	Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}, requiring no model modification unlike deep ensembles \cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} or MC-dropout \cite{gal2016dropout}.
24	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with structural utility functions.
25	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs; they attribute this to the mismatch between bag-of-unit utilities and compositional output structure, a diagnosis consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails for IE.
26	We extend their analysis by showing the specific failure mode: utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
27	Despite MBR's success in translation \cite{freitag2022high} and other generation tasks \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, this within-instance misalignment renders it ineffective for structured IE.
28	Conformal prediction \cite{fisch2021conformal, angelopoulos2021conformal} provides coverage guarantees; trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, venktesh2025trust} learn per-sample scoring that may bridge this gap.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency decoding \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning by majority voting over chain-of-thought samples, assuming a discrete answer space.
Extensions to free-form text use LLM-based comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, atomic sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or cross-sample hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
For test-time scaling \cite{zhang2025tts}, \citet{snell2025scaling} characterize compute scaling laws and \citet{brown2024monkeys} show best-of-$N$ gains across tasks.
Recent reward-free selectors include confidence-weighted voting \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc}, KL-based self-certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty}, adaptive sampling \cite{kim2026reasc}, ranked aggregation \cite{wang2025rankedvoting}, and latent-space consistency \cite{oh2025latentsc}.
Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings, echoing our finding that signal rankings shift with task complexity; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on output fusion rather than confidence-based selection.
All of the above target reasoning/QA with discrete answers or specific aggregation strategies.
Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap: strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$).

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE, corroborating our quality-estimation findings.
Their work leaves open three questions we address: (i)~whether structural matching improves on surface-level agreement (which they acknowledge ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs''); (ii)~whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection; and (iii)~whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient.
Soft Jaccard, the structural consistency measure used in our analysis, addresses (i) through type-aware bipartite matching with token-level span overlap; our selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) directly addresses (ii); and our three-dataset evaluation spanning easy (CoNLL) to hard (SciERC) tasks addresses (iii).
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses model confidence with inter-sample consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, josifoski2022genie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, wang2023instructuie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
Soft Jaccard uses standard tools (bipartite matching, token IoU) and is not itself a contribution; the contribution is the systematic comparison revealing when structural signals outperform surface-level agreement.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, selective abstention \cite{wen2025know}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs.
Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly.
Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}, requiring no model modification unlike deep ensembles \cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} or MC-dropout \cite{gal2016dropout}.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with structural utility functions.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs; they attribute this to the mismatch between bag-of-unit utilities and compositional output structure, a diagnosis consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails for IE.
We extend their analysis by showing the specific failure mode: utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Despite MBR's success in translation \cite{freitag2022high} and other generation tasks \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, this within-instance misalignment renders it ineffective for structured IE.
Conformal prediction \cite{fisch2021conformal, angelopoulos2021conformal} provides coverage guarantees; trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, venktesh2025trust} learn per-sample scoring that may bridge this gap.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances annotated for joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types).
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences with 4 entity types, where models achieve ${\approx}$91\% micro F1.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 social media instances with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries (52\% zero F1).
12	
13	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
14	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures.
15	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint has a minor train--test mismatch (empty thinking tokens); a quantitative analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
16	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows sublinear gains beyond $N{=}8$; 3-seed stability ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}) confirms identical signal rankings across seeds.}
17	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
18	
19	%% ============================================================
20	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
21	\label{sec:qe_results}
22	
23	\begin{table*}[t]
24	\centering
25	\small
26	\caption{Quality estimation across tasks and models (Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; $N{=}8$, seed${=}42$). Best value per column in \textbf{bold}. 47	\caption{Quality estimation heatmap (Spearman $\rho$) across five signals and four configurations. Left: full evaluation set; right: conditional set (non-zero F1 instances). On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC NER while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while LP RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.011$).}

Selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}).}
52	
53	\paragraph{Difficulty-dependent signal complementarity.}
54	On SciERC NER (6 types), structural signals lead: VC $\rho{=}0.379$, SJ $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and LP ($\rho{=}0.205$); on RE, VC extends this advantage ($\rho{=}0.350$; preliminary), but the remaining hierarchy reverses: multi-seed analysis shows LP rises above both SJ and FK (Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), likely because RE's 40\% zero-F1 rate creates a binary-outcome regime where generation confidence outperforms structural overlap.
55	The best NER AUROC reaches 0.816 (EM, CoNLL Qwen), indicating strong binary discriminative power; pairwise bootstrap CIs confirm the SJ--LP gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$, CI excludes zero) but the SJ--EM gap is marginal (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
56	
57	\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
58	Signal choice depends on use case: on CoNLL, EM leads AUROC (0.816) despite a middling $\rho$ (0.451), preferred for binary triage; this dissociation replicates across configurations (LP leads AUROC at 0.761 on CoNLL LLaMA yet trails in $\rho$).
59	
60	\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
61	On CoNLL (greedy F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$); this crossover---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates difficulty-dependent complementarity, consistent across model families.
62	On WNUT-17 (52\% zero F1), full-set VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$); all conditional signals collapse, suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency captures binary success/failure but not quality gradation.
63	
64	\paragraph{Conditional filtering.}
65	Restricting to non-zero F1 instances reshuffles signal rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right): EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$; preliminary), while structural signals drop substantially (VC NER: $0.379{\to}0.300$) and LP RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.011$ (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}).

3	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}

7	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
8	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
9	\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, is severely compressed within instances: the median LP range is 0.041 nats (IQR [0.024, 0.073]; Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}, Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}).

11	The gap holds even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).

22	The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency decoding \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning by majority voting over chain-of-thought samples, assuming a discrete answer space.
Extensions to free-form text use LLM-based comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, atomic sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or cross-sample hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
For test-time scaling \cite{zhang2025tts}, \citet{snell2025scaling} characterize compute scaling laws and \citet{brown2024monkeys} show best-of-$N$ gains across tasks.
Recent reward-free selectors include confidence-weighted voting \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc}, KL-based self-certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty}, adaptive sampling \cite{kim2026reasc}, ranked aggregation \cite{wang2025rankedvoting}, and latent-space consistency \cite{oh2025latentsc}.
Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings, echoing our finding that signal rankings shift with task complexity; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on output fusion rather than confidence-based selection.
All of the above target reasoning/QA with discrete answers or specific aggregation strategies.
Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap: strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$).

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE, corroborating our quality-estimation findings.
Their work leaves open three questions we address: (i)~whether structural matching improves on surface-level agreement (which they acknowledge ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs''); (ii)~whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection; and (iii)~whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient.
Soft Jaccard, the structural consistency measure used in our analysis, addresses (i) through type-aware bipartite matching with token-level span overlap; our selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) directly addresses (ii); and our three-dataset evaluation spanning easy (CoNLL) to hard (SciERC) tasks addresses (iii).
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses model confidence with inter-sample consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, josifoski2022genie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, wang2023instructuie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
Soft Jaccard uses standard tools (bipartite matching, token IoU) and is not itself a contribution; the contribution is the systematic comparison revealing when structural signals outperform surface-level agreement.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, selective abstention \cite{wen2025know}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs.
Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly.
Our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}, requiring no model modification unlike deep ensembles \cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} or MC-dropout \cite{gal2016dropout}.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with structural utility functions.

\section{Robustness Analysis}\label{app:robustness}

For these instances, F1 is trivially zero regardless of prediction quality, and consistency signals reflect agreement on the empty set rather than extraction quality---including them inflates or deflates Spearman $\rho$ depending on signal behavior at the boundary.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering

\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. LP shows the largest NER temperature effect ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.044$); RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data unavailable.}
\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.364 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.004.
FK NER $\rho$ drops by 0.022, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
LP exhibits the largest temperature effect on NER ($\rho{=}0.249$ at $T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $0.205$ at $T{=}1.0$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.044$), consistent with lower temperature concentrating probability mass and improving LP's discriminative power for quality estimation; RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data is not available.
Across all comparisons, the signal hierarchy is preserved at both temperatures on NER (SJ${>}$FK${>}$LP at $T{=}0.7$: $0.364{>}0.289{>}0.249$; at $T{=}1.0$: $0.360{>}0.267{>}0.205$).

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.411{\pm}0.010$ (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of $+0.047$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent---LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$---though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.042$ (range: $+0.039$ to $+0.044$) while LP gains only $+0.004$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is seed-dependent: Qwen SciERC gains range from $+0.005$ to $+0.023$ across seeds (mean $+0.016$), while LLaMA CoNLL yields $+0.039$ (3-seed mean); individual seed FK shifts vary substantially under the unified pipeline, so this should not be interpreted as a robust trend.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.030$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.034$).
SJ, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows seed-dependent variation that does not constitute a reliable trend, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.
At $N{=}16$, SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) while exhibiting lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$), making it a more stable alternative at higher sample sizes.

\paragraph{Transfer across model families.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct shows a similar SJ--FK ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.325{\pm}0.021$, FK $\rho{=}0.256{\pm}0.024$, $\Delta\rho{=}0.069$; permutation $p{=}0.06$, borderline).
On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-LP advantage holds across all four tested NER settings: Qwen SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.409$ vs.\ LP 0.239, $\Delta{=}{+}0.170$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ LP 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$),\footnote{Qwen CoNLL $N{=}16$ was not recomputed under the unified pipeline; LP $\rho{=}0.328$ may differ slightly from the registry value (0.315) due to instance filtering.} LLaMA SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ LP 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.474{\pm}0.009$ vs.\ LP $0.311{\pm}0.003$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.163$).

\section{Calibration Analysis}\label{app:calibration}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_reliability}
\caption{Reliability diagrams on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Top: mean F1 vs.\ binned confidence; bottom: instance counts per bin. Left: NER; right: RE. NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE shows greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), reflecting the difficulty of calibrating confidence for compound extraction tasks.}
\label{fig:reliability}
\end{figure*}

Reliability diagrams use 10 equal-width bins.
NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), indicating that translating consistency scores into calibrated confidence estimates is feasible for NER but remains challenging for compound extraction tasks.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{SJ normalizer robustness.}
Equation~\ref{eq:sj} uses $\max(|g_i|, |g_j|)$ as the denominator; an alternative is the union size $|g_i \cup g_j|$.
On SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, seed${=}42$), the two normalizers yield nearly identical quality estimation: $\rho_{\max}{=}0.360$ vs.\ $\rho_{\cup}{=}0.365$ ($\Delta\rho{=}0.005$, $\Delta$AUROC${=}0.003$); on CoNLL, $\rho_{\max}{=}0.431$ vs.\ $\rho_{\cup}{=}0.432$ ($\Delta\rho{<}0.001$).
The normalizer choice has negligible impact on results.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, consistent with the NER structural advantage; on full-set RE, however, the SJ--FK difference is non-significant ($\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.005$, $p{=}0.53$; preliminary).
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{WNUT-17 full signal analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17.
VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$) on the full set, but conditional analysis (non-zero F1 instances) reveals this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary: conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ ($p{=}0.49$).
LP shows the reverse pattern: full-set $\rho{=}{-}0.410$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.350$, the highest among all signals on the conditional set.
This inversion confirms that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

LP exhibits strong negative full-set $\rho$; its conditional $\rho$ reverses to the highest among all signals, confirming that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.}

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to four additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of greedy (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On CoNLL, 57--88\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect (greedy F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure; selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

CoNLL shows especially tight clustering where greedy already exceeds 0.90.}
\label{tab:cross_selection}

\toprule
Config & $n$ & Greedy & Oracle & SJ & FK & EM & LP & VC \\
\midrule

LLaMA/SciERC $N{=}16$ & 529 & .645 & .806 & \textbf{.649} & \textbf{.649} & .640 & .646 & .640 \\

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over greedy ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions---high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence---signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:

\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.

\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
The 4--5 thinking tokens contribute an estimated LP shift of 0.001 nats to the per-token log-probability average, representing 2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range (0.041 nats).
This shift is too small to alter LP-based rankings.

\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.

\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\section{LP Selection Failure Stability}\label{app:lp_failure_stability}

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ greedy F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46), indicating that failures are partially systematic---driven by instance complexity---but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), confirming a stable failure core.

\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher greedy F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429), indicating that LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well---precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.

\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (greedy F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (greedy NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs---a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}), not evidence against signal utility.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
4	On discrete-answer tasks, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains---+18~pp on GSM8K \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}---and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
5	These results assume that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs; for tasks with a single answer, majority voting is the selector.
6	But information extraction (IE) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
7	Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?
8	
9	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
10	Self-consistency methods for reasoning \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
11	\citet{yao2026consistency} examine consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE; our work extends theirs with structural matching, a selection analysis, and a difficulty gradient.
12	
13	Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): consistency signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) but fail at sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom.
14	Four of five signals are instance-level by construction; log-probability, the only per-sample signal, is too compressed to discriminate (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), though where compression is mitigated, selection recovers gains (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
